The company maintains significant operations across the United States, Europe, and Asia, with secondary presence in Brazil, Mexico, and Canada.

The filing discloses $165.8 million in negative cumulative adjustments to estimated profitability across defense programs in 2025, with the CH-53K helicopter contract accounting for $155.9 million. The CH-53K impairment included a $147.3 million adjustment in Q3 2025 driven by greater-than-planned labor content and higher material inputs, plus a $98.0 million loss reserve adjustment. The company also faces pending litigation related to alleged exposure to asbestos-containing products with unquantified financial exposure. Separately, Albany Engineered Composites achieved U.S. Department of Defense Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification Level 2 in December 2025 and must pursue Level 3 certification for certain future defense programs. The company divested Arcari in 2025 and is pursuing the sale of its structures assembly business at the Amelia Earhart Drive facility in Salt Lake City, with those AEC assets classified as held-for-sale as of year-end.

The Machine Clothing segment faces structural headwinds from consolidation in the global paper industry and reduced demand from digital media displacement. Demand for newsprint and printing paper has contracted, and shift toward alternative packaging has pressured the segment. Competition from Chinese manufacturers intensifies particularly in that market. Customer concentration in Machine Clothing remains diffuse, with no single customer exceeding 10% of segment revenues. In Engineered Composites, SAFRAN Group sales accounted for approximately 15% of consolidated net revenues in 2025, consisting primarily of fan blades and cases for CFM's LEAP engine; those LEAP revenues peaked above $210 million in 2019 but have declined sharply since. The company competes against larger aerospace suppliers with substantially greater resources. Long-term fixed-price contracts expose the company to cost pressures, as demonstrated by the CH-53K experience. Carbon fiber sourcing relies on multiple suppliers with customer mandates for specific sources, while approximately 20% of worldwide monofilament requirements are manufactured internally at the Homer, New York facility.

Forward initiatives include completing the multi-year Heimbach integration and realizing synergies, executing the eight-year remaining CH-53K contract, strategic review of the Salt Lake City facility, advancing 3D-woven technology development, and establishing a New Business Ventures group targeting meaningful revenue growth by 2027. The company completed facility closures in South Korea, Switzerland, and is closing operations in Italy, France, and the United Kingdom in 2025.

### EXPI [Critical]
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1495932/000110465926019145/expi-20251231x10k.htm)_

_Triggers: 1 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed; regulatory action: National Association of Realtors / U.S. Department of Justice; CFO changed during fiscal year._

eXp World Holdings operates a cloud-based real estate brokerage platform serving residential and commercial markets. The North American Realty segment handles brokerage, lead generation, and support services across the United States and Canada, and now includes FrameVR.io, a proprietary 3D immersive platform for agent collaboration and training added in Q1 2025. International Realty operates across 27 countries in the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Asia-Pacific, and South Africa. The company positions itself as the only global cloud-based real estate brokerage with scale, emphasizing low entry fees, stock ownership opportunities, and multi-tiered revenue-sharing compensation. A third segment, Other Affiliated Services, publishes SUCCESS magazine and related media for agent and broker development. Revenue derives primarily from commissions on residential real estate transactions across all segments.

The company faces material headwinds from regulatory and litigation developments in its core market. In March 2024, the National Association of Realtors settlement agreement (resulting from DOJ action) imposed rule changes affecting MLS practices, cooperative compensation, and buyer agreements—the company must now comply with prohibitions on compensation offers listed on MLS and must obtain written buyer agreements before showings. Separately, eXp settled an antitrust class action lawsuit (1925 Hooper LLC, et al. v. The National Association of Realtors et al., Case No. 1:23-cv-05392-SEG, Northern District of Georgia) on December 9, 2024, agreeing to pay $34.0 million and implement business practice changes. The settlement received preliminary approval on May 23, 2025, but remains subject to final court approval and appeals. Additionally, the company recorded a $4.93 million impairment charge in fiscal 2024 related to its Virbela business and Other Affiliated Services segment assets. Leadership changes during the year include Jesse Hill's appointment as Chief Financial Officer, Carrie Lysenko as Chief Technology Officer of eXp Realty, and Holly Mabery as Chief Brokerage Officer of eXp Realty.

The business operates in a cyclical, economically sensitive market. eXp identifies material disadvantages including elevated mortgage rates that reduce purchasing power, housing inventory imbalances, affordability challenges from rising living costs, and material decreases in average brokerage commission rates beyond its control. The company competes against local, regional, and national residential brokerages, discount brokers, listing aggregators, non-traditional platforms, and technology companies recruiting experienced software developers. Competition includes brokerages with greater financial resources. The company's agent classification and compensation structure remain subject to evolving legal standards and regulatory scrutiny, presenting ongoing compliance risks.

The company is advancing several initiatives: a Land and Ranch Division launching in Q2 2025, a Sports and Entertainment Division in Q4 2025, a CRM of Choice platform in Q3 2025, and the LYVVE global property search platform in Q4 2025. A Co-Sponsor Program allowing dual sponsorship launched in Q2 2025. No specific capital expenditure amounts or forward revenue guidance were disclosed.

### GOGO [Critical]
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1537054/000119312526082487/gogo-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: material weakness in internal controls disclosed; 2 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed; 2 regulatory action(s) disclosed._

Gogo Inc. operates as a single-segment provider of in-flight connectivity services across multiple satellite networks and frequency bands, serving business and military/government aviation customers. The company positions itself as the only multi-orbit, multi-band provider purpose-built for aviation, offering a comprehensive platform that includes ATG Broadband, GEO Broadband, narrowband satellite services, and the newly launched Gogo Galileo LEO Broadband Service alongside in-flight systems (AVANCE, Plane Simple, Satcom Direct Router and variants, FlightDeck Freedom) and engineering services. Operations center on North America, with the U.S., Canada, and Mexico as primary markets, though service extends to over 100 countries. The company distributes through established OEM relationships and a global dealer network.

A jury verdict in November 2025 awarded SmartSky $22.7 million in a patent infringement suit filed in February 2022, with post-trial briefing pending and appeal likely. Separately, a competitor filed an antitrust lawsuit in December 2024 alleging Gogo maintains an illegal monopoly over ATG broadband in-flight connectivity and blocks market entry. Beyond litigation, Gogo disclosed a material weakness in internal control over financial reporting and confirmed that disclosure controls and ICFR are not effective. The FCC Supply Chain Reimbursement Program approved approximately $334 million in reimbursements for ZTE equipment removal and replacement; Gogo filed roughly $98.4 million in claims and received $97.8 million as of February 1, 2026. The FCC imposed a May 8, 2026 completion deadline for Priority 1 participants, which includes Gogo, though the company expects to require additional extensions beyond that date.

Gogo faces a competitive field including Honeywell Aerospace, Collins Aerospace, SES, SpaceX, ViaSat, BAE Systems, General Dynamics, Telesat, L3Harris, Echostar, Hughes Network Systems, and Northrop Grumman across equipment provision, GEO and LEO satellite services, resale, and government communications. Top ten customers represented approximately 29% of 2025 service revenue, while no single customer exceeded 10% of revenue. The company self-discloses substantial debt limiting financial flexibility, dependence on single-source satellite network providers, reliance on third-party equipment suppliers for critical components, supply chain disruption risks, and the material weakness in internal controls. Manufacturing and repair facilities operate in the U.S. and Canada with globally sourced components and shared antenna design responsibility with third-party vendors.

Gogo completed a $415.5 million acquisition of Satcom Direct, LLC and affiliates in 2024. Forward initiatives include Gogo Galileo LEO broadband service launch in Q1 2025, Gogo 5G network launch in Q4 2025, LTE network transition for AVANCE customers expected in 2026, and FCC Reimbursement Program completion targeted for May 8, 2026.

### GPK [Critical]
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1408075/000140807526000009/gpk-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: material weakness in internal controls disclosed; CFO changed during fiscal year; CEO changed during fiscal year._

Graphic Packaging Holding Co manufactures paperboard packaging across two primary segments: Americas Paperboard Packaging, which supplies cartons, multipack cartons, trays, carriers, canisters, cups, bowls, lids and food containers to consumer packaged goods companies and foodservice operators; and International Paperboard Packaging, which serves similar end markets primarily in Europe. The company operates across the Americas, Europe, and Asia Pacific, with the first two regions as primary markets. It positions itself competitively through integrated paperboard manufacturing and converting operations, proprietary carton designs and packaging machine technologies, and a patent portfolio exceeding 3,100 patents. Stated competitive advantages center on design customization, recyclability innovation, and strong customer relationships, though the company faces broad competition from Smurfit WestRock plc and manufacturers of plastic, shrink-wrap, corrugated, foam, and molded fiber alternatives.

The company disclosed a material weakness in internal controls and stated that disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting were not effective during the fiscal year. Both the Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer changed positions during the period, creating significant transition risk during a time when control environment effectiveness is in question. These governance changes coincided with the company's disclosure of material weakness, raising questions about the scope and magnitude of underlying control deficiencies and whether leadership transitions may have contributed to or exacerbated control environment challenges.

Graphic Packaging faces material structural constraints that shape operational risk. The company has high debt levels that management identifies as limiting financial flexibility. Raw material cost volatility presents a documented exposure, with limited ability to pass increases through to customers; the company sources pine and hardwood pulp from private landowners and open markets near Louisiana, Georgia and Texas facilities, and recovered fiber from external suppliers and internal operations. No single customer or vendor exceeds 10% of purchases or sales, reducing concentration risk, but this breadth does not offset the company's vulnerability to economic downturns affecting customer demand or its exposure to foreign currency exchange fluctuations. The company has undertaken significant facility rationalization, closing recycled paperboard manufacturing operations in Middletown Ohio (May 2025), East Angus Quebec (December 2025), and Kalamazoo Michigan (2024), alongside a prior closure in Tama Iowa (Q2 2023). In 2024, the company divested operations to Clearwater Paper Corporation for $711 million, while completing acquisitions of Greif Packaging LLC and Bell Incorporated for $100 million and $262 million respectively in 2023.

The company is constructing a recycled paperboard manufacturing facility in Waco, Texas as a forward capital initiative. Sustainability commitments under its Vision 2030 framework target 90% renewable fuel use in wood fiber paperboard manufacturing, 50% purchased renewable electricity by 2030, and 100% forest products from sustainably managed sources, with greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets aligned to 2032.

### GT [Critical]
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/42582/000162828026006708/gt-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: $674M+ impairment disclosed; 4 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed; regulatory action: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency._

Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co manufactures and distributes tires across a broad range of applications—automobiles, trucks, buses, aircraft, motorcycles, and farm equipment—alongside tire retreading services, repair offerings, and chemical products. The company operates through three geographic segments: Americas (North, Central, and South America), Europe, Middle East and Africa, and Asia Pacific. Its primary markets are the United States, Europe, and China. Goodyear competes globally against Bridgestone, Michelin, Continental, Hankook, Kumho, Pirelli, Sumitomo, Toyo, Yokohama, and Dunlop, as well as various regional producers and Asian imports. The company positions itself on brand recognition, a network of approximately 750 retail outlets, manufacturing presence across 19 countries with 49 facilities, and scale as one of the world's largest commercial truck service center operators. Stated disadvantages include a manufacturing footprint that is less cost-competitive than principal competitors, periodic capacity constraints on higher-margin products, capital intensity below competitors, substantial fixed costs, and exposure to commodity price, currency, and international political volatility.

The 2025 filing reflects significant operational and financial stress. Goodyear recorded a $674 million non-cash goodwill impairment charge for its North America reporting unit, triggered by continued industry disruption, a reduced near-term and long-term outlook, and sustained stock price decline. The company simultaneously completed a series of major asset sales: the OTR tire business to Yokohama for $905 million (February 2025), the Dunlop brand to Sumitomo Rubber for $526 million (May 2025), and the Chemical Business for $650 million (October 2025). These transactions represent a material reshaping of the business portfolio. Goodyear faces four pending litigation matters: approximately 30,400 asbestos claimants with unspecified damages sought; a European Commission antitrust investigation initiated by unannounced inspections in January 2024; U.S. antitrust civil litigation (with a motion to dismiss granted February 25, 2025, followed by amended complaint motions April 11, 2025); and an EPA Notice of Violation dated August 15, 2025 alleging Clean Air Act violations at the former Beaumont, Texas chemical facility with potential penalties exceeding $1 million.

The company's structural position reflects significant operational challenges. Goodyear sources synthetic rubber from Beaumont and Houston facilities transferred October 31, 2025; natural rubber from world markets; and commodities like carbon black, steel cord, and fabrics substantially from independent suppliers. The company discloses self-assessed disadvantages including manufacturing cost-competitiveness gaps relative to principal competitors, lower capital intensity as a ratio to sales, and substantial fixed-cost exposure creating disproportionate income fluctuation during downturns. Facility disruptions are material: announced closures of tire plants in Fulda and Fürstenwalde (Germany) and Kariega (South Africa); planned elimination of commercial tire production at Danville, Virginia; and significant fire damage at the Debica, Poland facility causing temporary shutdown. The company carries significant debt obligations it characterizes as restricting growth flexibility.

Capital plans total $825 million in planned capex. Key initiatives center on prior restructuring: the Goodyear Forward plan completed in 2025 achieved $1.5 billion in annual cost savings. Forward commitments include 100% renewable electricity in manufacturing by 2030.

### HP [Critical]
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/46765/000004676525000071/hp-20250930.htm)_

_Triggers: material weakness in internal controls disclosed; $133M impairment disclosed; acquisition $2.0B disclosed._

Helmerich & Payne operates a global onshore and offshore drilling services business organized across four segments. North America Solutions runs what the company describes as the largest and most technologically advanced AC drive drilling rig fleet in North America, concentrated in the Permian Basin and Eagle Ford Shale. International Solutions conducts land drilling operations across the Middle East (Saudi Arabia, Oman, Bahrain, Kuwait), South America (Argentina, Colombia), Europe (Germany), and Northern Africa. Offshore Solutions operates platform rigs in U.S. federal waters and manages asset-light contract operations in the North Sea, Norwegian Sea, Caspian Sea, Angola, Azerbaijan, and Canada. The Other segment encompasses BENTEC manufacturing and engineering operations across four facilities, real estate holdings in Tulsa, Oklahoma, and captive insurance operations. The company positions itself on technological differentiation, citing its FlexRig platform with continuous innovation since 1998, automated monitoring through 24/7 Remote Operations Centers, and vertically integrated manufacturing capabilities.

The filing discloses a material weakness in internal controls over financial reporting, with disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting both assessed as ineffective. Additionally, Helmerich & Payne recorded $132.7 million in goodwill impairment charges against the International Solutions reporting unit and $59.5 million against BENTEC in fiscal 2025. Most significantly, the company completed its $2.0 billion acquisition of KCA Deutag International Limited in January 2025. The company faces integration risks from this transaction, which it acknowledges explicitly. Management plans to resume seven Saudi Arabia rigs in the first half of calendar 2026 and to rebrand the Kenera business unit as BENTEC following September 2025. Cost reduction initiatives include a workforce reduction plan and $50 million in targeted general and administrative expense cuts.

Customer concentration poses material risk across segments. The largest consolidated customer represented 12.0% of revenues in fiscal 2025 and 11.0% in 2024. Within segments, concentration is sharper: the largest North America Solutions customer accounts for 18.2% of segment revenues, the largest International Solutions customer 32.3%, and the largest Offshore Solutions customer 45.2% of segment revenues. Saudi Arabia operations derive all revenues from the national oil company. The company faces significant disadvantages including a substantial portion of available rigs not under contract and a surplus of drilling rigs in many markets. Fixed operating costs do not decline proportionally with reduced utilization. The company names Nabors Industries Ltd., Patterson-UTI Energy Inc., Precision Drilling Corporation, and Blake International Rigs LLC as competitors, and notes it competes against many regional operators and lower-specification rig providers. Supply chain concentration exists in BENTEC facilities: Germany serves as the main engineering hub, with critical regional operations in Saudi Arabia, Oman, and Ukraine.

Capital expenditures are planned in the range of $280 million to $320 million, centered on $300 million. The acquisition integration represents the near-term strategic focus, with plans to integrate KCA Deutag rigs into the company's digital ecosystem and RSMS monitoring infrastructure.

### IIPR [Critical]
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1677576/000167757626000001/iipr-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: going concern language present; 3 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed; regulatory action: SEC._

INNOVATIVE INDUSTRIAL PROPERTIES INC owns and leases industrial and commercial real estate to state-licensed cannabis operators, along with a growing life science investment portfolio. Its Cannabis Portfolio Segment provides specialized facilities—cultivation operations, retail dispensaries, and hybrid facilities—to regulated cannabis businesses across 19 states. The company positions itself as a capital solutions provider for operators with limited access to traditional financing, offering sale-leaseback arrangements and citing advantages in management expertise, contractual rent escalations, rigorous underwriting, and established relationships within the cannabis and real estate sectors. The Life Science Portfolio Segment deploys capital through preferred equity and credit facilities, representing a stated growth component. Primary markets are Florida, Illinois, Massachusetts, Michigan, and Pennsylvania; secondary exposure spans Arizona, California, Colorado, and nine other states.

INNOVATIVE INDUSTRIAL PROPERTIES disclosed going concern language in this filing, signaling material uncertainty about the company's ability to continue operations. The company faces three pending litigation matters: two purported securities class action lawsuits alleging false or misleading statements by the company and certain officers, and derivative lawsuits against officers and directors asserting breach of fiduciary duty and mismanagement. Additionally, the SEC's Denver Regional Office issued a subpoena as part of a formal investigation concerning matters similar to those alleged in the securities lawsuits. Most concretely, PharmaCann—a material tenant—has defaulted on leases covering nine properties across New York, Illinois, Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Colorado, with $29.2 million in total amounts due for base rent, property management fees, and estimated tax and insurance. The company recovered possession of a Michigan property in April 2025 and a Dwight, Illinois facility in December 2025, both formerly leased to PharmaCann, though it has since re-leased the Michigan property. The company also took possession of four California properties through deed in lieu of foreclosure in September 2025 and recognized a $3.5 million impairment loss on a Palm Springs property sold in June 2025.

The business model carries structural vulnerabilities particular to cannabis real estate. The company disclosed that federal illegality of cannabis creates enforcement uncertainty, tenant financial distress is driven by market dynamics including declining unit pricing, and cannabis-focused real estate has limited liquidity and reusability. The company has ten named material tenants—including Trulieve, Curaleaf, Green Thumb Industries, Cresco Labs, and Ascend Wellness Holdings—without disclosed concentration thresholds, creating exposure to operator-level financial stress. Geographic concentration in cannabis-focused states amplifies regulatory and demand risk. Competitors span independent investors, hedge funds, other REITs, hard money lenders, and the operators themselves, fragmenting the market.

The company committed $100 million to a joint venture with IQHQ REIT and completed a $50 million asset purchase from IQHQ in 2025, with a pending $120 million additional asset purchase. It also sold three properties for combined proceeds of $11.3 million in 2025 and plans to invest up to $170 million in IQHQ preferred stock through Q2 2027 as part of life science portfolio expansion. Notes due in May 2026 require refinancing prior to maturity.

### MSEX [Critical]
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/66004/000162828026009777/msex-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: 1 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed; regulatory action: USEPA; auditor changed during fiscal year._

Middlesex Water Co operates two business segments delivering water and wastewater services across New Jersey and Delaware. The regulated segment provides residential, commercial, industrial, fire protection, and wholesale water services alongside wastewater collection and treatment through five branded systems: Middlesex System, Tidewater System, Pinelands Water, Pinelands Wastewater, and Southern Shores. The non-regulated segment offers contract operations and maintenance services to municipal and private water and wastewater systems across the broader region. The company positions itself on exclusive franchises in Tidewater service areas, established wholesale contracts with municipalities, interconnected regional water systems, and adequate water supply sources. However, the business faces material structural constraints: revenue depends entirely on regulatory commission rate approvals in New Jersey and Delaware, water availability is vulnerable to drought and aquifer depletion, and the company operates in concentrated geographies with exposure to weather volatility affecting customer demand.

Three regulatory matters and a litigation settlement reshape the company's near-term financial and operational profile. In April 2024, the USEPA finalized drinking water regulations for PFAS, establishing maximum contaminant levels lower than New Jersey's current standards and requiring water systems to complete initial monitoring by April 2027 and implement treatment solutions by April 2029 if levels exceed the new MCLs. Middlesex Water disclosed multi-district litigation against PFAS manufacturers; settlements with 3M Company, DuPont de Nemours, Tyco Fire Products, and BASF Corporation have received final approval, providing some recovery of remediation costs. On the rate side, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities approved a $14.5 million base rate increase for Middlesex and Pinelands effective February 23, 2026, and the Delaware Public Service Commission approved a $5.5 million increase for Tidewater effective July 3, 2025. The NJBPU also approved the merger of Pinelands into Middlesex through corporate reorganization. The company changed auditors during the fiscal year to PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP.

Capital deployment centers on PFAS treatment infrastructure and system modernization. The company plans a $255 million upgrade to the Carl J. Olsen Surface Water Treatment Plant (CJO Plant) between 2026 and 2028 to integrate PFAS removal. Planned capex totals $126 million, with the RENEW Program allocating $12 million annually for water main replacement, a $9 million Bethany Bay water treatment facility in the Tidewater System, and elevated storage tank construction. In 2025, Middlesex completed the $4.6 million acquisition of water assets from the Town of Ocean View, Delaware, and announced a merger with Pinelands Water and Pinelands Wastewater. These moves consolidate the Delaware footprint and integrate regulated operations while positioning for compliance with tightening federal water quality standards within the three-to-five-year regulatory timeline.

### NWL [Critical]
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/814453/000081445326000008/nwl-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: $345M impairment disclosed; 1 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed; regulatory action: SEC._

Newell Brands Inc. operates across three segments serving consumer and commercial markets globally. Home and Commercial Solutions designs and distributes household products spanning kitchen appliances, food storage, cookware, cutlery, home fragrance, and commercial cleaning solutions alongside closet organization and hygiene systems. Learning and Development produces writing instruments, markers, highlighters, art products, activity-based items, labeling solutions, and baby gear and infant care products. Outdoor and Recreation markets technical apparel, beverageware, and active lifestyle products for outdoor activities. The company maintains a global footprint across over 150 countries, with North America as its primary market and Europe, Middle East and Africa, Asia-Pacific, and Latin America as secondary regions. Newell positions itself on a portfolio of established brands, broad multi-product offerings, experienced management, strong retail relationships, and competitive cost structures.

The company disclosed a $345 million impairment of indefinite-lived intangible assets in fiscal 2025, comprising $163 million and $127 million in tradename write-downs in the Home and Commercial Solutions segment and $50 million in the Learning and Development segment. This represents the third consecutive year of significant impairments ($339 million in 2023, $345 million in 2024). Concurrently, Newell undertook facility restructuring, closing approximately 20 Yankee Candle stores in January 2026 as part of broader cost reduction efforts. An SEC settlement from 2023 relating to prior sales practices and accounting matters between Q3 2016 and Q2 2017 resulted in a $13 million financial exposure. These events collectively reflect sustained challenges in asset valuations and operational performance across multiple business units.

Newell faces meaningful structural constraints. Amazon and Walmart Inc. and subsidiaries represent concentrated customer exposure at 17% and 13% of net sales respectively in 2025. The baby business unit within Learning and Development relies on a single source of supply for products comprising a majority of its sales, creating discrete supply chain vulnerability. Sourcing spans China and over 50 countries, exposing the company to tariff and trade policy risk. The competitive landscape includes large manufacturers, digitally native brands, specialty retailers, and private label competitors, with the company explicitly disclosing disadvantages including dominant retailer negotiating power, pricing pressures, customer consolidation reducing leverage, e-commerce lowering barriers for competitors, and a high debt burden limiting operational flexibility.

Newell is executing multiple forward initiatives: a productivity plan involving workforce reduction of over 900 employees in 2026, ERP consolidation and SKU optimization, tariff mitigation through manufacturing relocation, and organizational realignment of global brand management completed in 2025. The company completed an asset sale involving a joint venture equity interest in 2025. No revenue or earnings guidance was provided for forward periods.

### NX [Critical]
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1423221/000142322125000100/nx-20251031.htm)_

_Triggers: material weakness in internal controls disclosed; $302M impairment disclosed; 2 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed._

Quanex Building Products CORP manufactures and distributes component products for the building products industry across three segments: Hardware Solutions (window and door hardware and screens), Extruded Solutions (insulating glass spacers, vinyl profiles, seals, and weatherstripping), and Custom Solutions (wood, mixing, and building access solutions). The company serves original equipment manufacturers and retailers with a broad product portfolio spanning window and door components, kitchen and bath cabinet parts, vinyl decking, solar panel sealants, and commercial access solutions. Operations span North America and the United Kingdom as primary geographies, with secondary presence in Germany, Mexico, Italy, Canada, and other European markets. Quanex positions itself on cost-effective production, design expertise, proprietary process technology, patent protection for vinyl extrusion products, and just-in-time delivery capabilities. It claims to be the largest supplier to OEMs in the U.S. wood business.

A $302.3 million goodwill impairment recorded in the third quarter of fiscal 2025 (nine months ended July 31, 2025) reflects a material reset of valuation following the company's segment restructuring and a stock price decline driven by weaker consumer confidence and industry uncertainty. More significantly, the company disclosed a material weakness in internal controls over financial reporting, with disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting both rendered ineffective. These control deficiencies create substantive financial reporting risk going forward. The filing also surfaces two pending litigation matters: a shareholder class action (Zanol v. Quanex Building Products Corporation et al., filed September 19, 2025 in U.S. District Court, Southern District of Texas, Case No. 4:25-cv-04453) alleging securities law violations related to public disclosures in 2025 concerning window and door operations in Mexico, with unspecified damages sought; and multiple remaining claims related to alleged defects in a commercial sealant product manufactured in the 2000s, which the company believes were meritless and contends it would prevail at trial.

Quanex carries structural vulnerabilities that amplify the impact of current headwinds. The company is explicitly dependent on relatively few large customers for certain business lines, creating concentration risk. OEMs possess substantial pricing leverage over the company, and larger international suppliers similarly hold leverage over customer relationships. The competitive field is fragmented, spanning Assa Abloy, Roto, Veka, Epwin, and numerous smaller regional players, but competition centers on price, quality, delivery, and custom specifications—a zero-margin dynamic. Demand is inherently cyclical, tied to housing starts and remodeling activity. Short lead times provide limited backlog visibility. The business also faces vulnerability to raw material price fluctuations and supply disruptions, and customers may vertically integrate fenestration operations, directly eroding demand.

The company completed the $504.1 million acquisition of Tyman plc in 2024 and an earlier $91.3 million asset purchase from Lauren International and Meteor-US-Beteiligungs in 2022. Current strategic initiatives focus on Tyman integration and cross-selling opportunities, European energy efficiency retrofit programs and EU directives, and the segment restructuring already executed. No specific capex guidance or forward financial targets were disclosed.

### PENN [Critical]
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/921738/000092173826000008/penn-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: $825M+ impairment disclosed; 1 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed; 1 regulatory action(s) disclosed._

PENN Entertainment operates a diversified portfolio of 42 gaming and racing properties across 19 states, plus Ontario, Canada, organized into four regional segments (Northeast, South, West, Midwest) and an Interactive division. The company's core business centers on traditional gaming—slot machines and table games—supplemented by food and beverage, hotel operations, and racing. The Interactive segment encompasses online sports betting, online casino operations, social gaming, retail sportsbook management, and sports media assets including theScore. PENN positions itself as a market leader in retail casino operations with a claimed competitive advantage through its proprietary digital sports betting and iCasino platform, in-house content studio, and the PENN Play loyalty program, which has over 33 million members. The company operates across North American markets with primary exposure to the Northeast, South, West, and Midwest regions of the United States.

PENN Entertainment recorded an $825 million goodwill impairment in its Interactive segment in 2025 driven by the early termination of its ESPN Sportsbook Agreement and resulting realignment of its digital strategy. This impairment reflects a material reassessment of the company's digital betting business following the ESPN partnership exit. Beyond this charge, the company disclosed additional impairments totaling $120.3 million across multiple segments: $98.3 million in gaming licenses and trademarks at Northeast, South, and West properties attributable to increased supply from legislation expansion and regional economic pressures; a $15 million trademark impairment related to the strategic rebranding of Ameristar Council Bluffs to Hollywood Casino; and a $7 million goodwill impairment in the South segment. In governance, three new board members—Heather Ace, Jeffrey Fox, and Fabio Schiavolin—were appointed in February 2026 under a cooperation agreement with HG Vora Capital Management following settlement of litigation. Additionally, the Colorado Limited Gaming Control Commission imposed a licensing condition in 2025 requiring a suitability determination before any investor may acquire or exercise control or influence over the company's Colorado gaming operations.

The company faces material structural constraints that distinguish its risk profile. A stated disadvantage explicitly highlights dependence on certain geographic regions for significant revenue, and reliance on third parties for essential online sports betting and iCasino services—a vulnerability underscored by the ESPN partnership termination. Competition spans a broad spectrum from established casinos and state-sponsored lotteries to prediction markets and illegal gaming operations, with PENN acknowledging competitive pressure from growing alternative gaming forms. The company's cash flow flexibility is limited by significant interest and rent payment obligations. Operationally, PENN closed the Freehold Raceway facility in December 2024 and sold the property in June 2025, while also shuttering the OTW facility in New Jersey in December 2024, signaling strategic rationalization of underperforming assets.

Planned capital expenditures total $445 million. Key initiatives include opening the Aurora Project land-based casino and Columbus hotel tower in late Q2 2026, the relocation of Hollywood Casino Council Bluffs in late 2027 to early 2028, and recent completions including the Joliet land-based facility (August 2025) and the M Resort second hotel tower adding 375 rooms (December 2025).

### RUN [Critical]
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1469367/000162828026012289/run-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: $3.1B+ impairment disclosed; 1 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed; 1 regulatory action(s) disclosed._

Sunrun Inc. designs, installs, owns, and maintains residential solar and battery storage systems across the United States, with a smaller presence in Puerto Rico. The company operates through a single reportable segment—Residential Solar and Storage—offering systems via customer leases and power purchase agreements, as well as direct sales. Its product suite extends beyond core solar to include battery storage, inverters, racking systems, roof repair, EV chargers, home energy management services, grid services, and renewable energy credits. Sunrun positions itself as the largest fleet operator of residential energy systems in the United States, leveraging a scalable platform with multi-channel distribution, proprietary BrightPath software, access to low-cost capital and tax equity funding, and a strong partner network. Customer credit quality averages above 740 FICO scores.

A $3.1 billion goodwill impairment charge in the fourth quarter of 2024 reflects a sharp decline in market capitalization relative to book equity value, requiring a full write-down of previously recorded goodwill. The company identified this through an interim quantitative assessment using an income approach and market cap comparison. Additionally, a regulatory action initiated by the California Contractors State License Board in June 2023 now presents operational exposure: the CSLB adopted a rule on April 18, 2024 (effective October 1, 2024) requiring C-10 license holders for energy storage system repair and retrofit work. The rule has been challenged and is currently subject to a preliminary injunction blocking enforcement pending case resolution. A settled administrative proceeding from 2021 involving the CSLB and certain Sunrun officers related to an installation accident by affiliate Horizon Solar Power resulted in citations and withdrawal without admission of wrongdoing.

Structural constraints shape material business risk. The company depends on a limited number of manufacturers and suppliers for solar panels, inverters, and batteries, creating supply chain vulnerability. Geographic dependencies on China for lithium-ion battery cells and Vietnam for tariff-subject components introduce exposure to trade restrictions and cost volatility. California represents over 45 percent of the customer base, concentrating geographic risk significantly. Competitive pressures span traditional utilities, other residential solar installers with similar models, community solar projects, finance-driven aggregators, large construction firms, and lenders offering solar financing alternatives. Key stated disadvantages include reliance on government incentives and tax credits subject to expiration or reduction, tariff exposure, declining equipment costs creating pricing uncertainty, and regulatory changes to net metering that reduce customer value propositions.

Forward initiatives include expanding the grid services business to position distributed systems as virtual power plants, pursuing solar-plus-storage growth in California, advancing home electrification through EV chargers and battery retrofits, and opportunistically acquiring previously installed solar systems. The company completed an asset purchase from a third-party investor in 2025, adding to prior acquisitions of Vivint Solar in 2020 and a joint venture with SK E&S Co., Ltd. that same year.

Peabody Energy Corp mines and sells thermal and metallurgical coal from 16 active operations across the United States and Australia. The company operates four segments: Seaborne Thermal (low-sulfur, high Btu coal from New South Wales surface mines), Seaborne Metallurgical (hard and semi-coking coal from Queensland, New South Wales, and Alabama using surface and underground extraction), Powder River Basin (thermal coal from Wyoming surface mines with lower sulfur content), and Other U.S. Thermal (thermal coal from Illinois, Indiana, New Mexico, and Colorado). Peabody positions itself as a leading producer with long-term supply agreements covering the majority of sales, modern loading facilities, and strong relationships with North American and Australian rail and port operators. The company serves customers across the United States and Australia primarily, with secondary markets in China, India, Indonesia, Colombia, Russia, South Africa, Mongolia, Mozambique, and Canada. Its five largest customers represented 25% of coal supply agreement revenue in 2025, with the single largest customer contributing approximately 8%.

The filing discloses pending arbitration initiated by Anglo American subsidiaries challenging Peabody's termination of a $75 million metallurgical coal portfolio acquisition in 2024. Anglo alleges the termination was wrongful and contests whether an ignition event at Moranbah North mine on March 31, 2025 constituted a Material Adverse Change, seeking unspecified damages and costs. The company faces meaningful regulatory pressure. In February 2026, the EPA finalized rescission of the 2009 endangerment finding and repealed all GHG emission standards for fossil fuel-fired power plants—reversing prior regulatory posture but introducing uncertainty around future enforcement. The OWCP finalized a rule in December 2024 on coal operator self-insurance that could require Peabody to post approximately $40 million in additional security for black lung liabilities, though the Trump Administration indicated in February 2025 that a 60-day deadline is no longer applicable. Australian labour hire legislation passed in December 2023 has increased operating costs at Coppabella and Metropolitan mines.

Peabody confronts substantial structural headwinds. U.S. coal power capacity has retired 46% since 2010, with an additional 3 gigawatts retiring in 2025. Thermal coal demand is pressured by natural gas competition strengthened by domestic U.S. production. The company carries take-or-pay arrangements totaling $1.0 billion, converting variable costs to fixed obligations. Reclamation bonding requirements in the U.S. and Australia are substantial. Financial institutions' ESG concerns have restricted Peabody's capital markets access, and limited availability of surety bonds and letters of credit from banks avoiding fossil fuels constrains operational flexibility. The competitive landscape includes diversified producers (Alliance Resource Partners, Warrior Met Coal, Glencore, BHP, Anglo American) and alternative electricity sources (natural gas, renewables, nuclear), plus competing seaborne supplies from Indonesia, Russia, South Africa, Canada, Mongolia, and Mozambique.

Peabody has budgeted $340 million in capital expenditure. Key initiatives include Centurion Mine commencing full-scale longwall production in February 2026, and a rare earth element recovery pilot plant funded at $6.25 million in Wyoming, testing mineral recovery and developing processing flowsheets.

Cal-Maine Foods is the largest producer and distributor of shell eggs in the United States, operating across 40 states and Puerto Rico. The company operates a single segment encompassing production, packaging, marketing and distribution of shell eggs, egg products and prepared foods. Its product portfolio spans conventional shell eggs; specialty varieties including cage-free, organic, brown, free-range, pasture-raised and nutritionally enhanced eggs; liquid and frozen egg products; and prepared foods such as hard-cooked eggs, egg wraps, protein pancakes, crepes, waffles, scrambled eggs, frozen omelets and egg patties. Cal-Maine positions itself on vertical integration, modern in-line facilities, established customer relationships, and proximity to customers as sources of cost advantage and operational efficiency.

The company faces two material legal exposures. In fiscal 2024, Cal-Maine accrued a $19.6 million loss contingency related to pending antitrust litigation with a jury decision already rendered. More significantly, in March 2025 the Department of Justice issued a civil investigative demand to the company as part of a broader antitrust investigation into causes of nationwide egg price increases. The DOJ has also filed a separate lawsuit against the State of California alleging that cage-free laws violate the Supremacy Clause and contribute to higher egg prices. These concurrent investigations and litigation create regulatory and reputational risk, though the second matter does not directly implicate Cal-Maine as a defendant.

Cal-Maine's business model carries substantial structural vulnerabilities. Walmart Inc. and Sam's Club alone account for 33.6% of net sales in fiscal 2025, while the top three customers collectively represent 49.2% of sales—a concentration that grants major retailers significant bargaining leverage. The company explicitly discloses that customer consolidation has produced larger buyers with increased purchasing power and identifies this as a disadvantage. The shell egg market is intensely competitive and highly fragmented, competing against numerous domestic producers as well as restaurants, grocery stores and convenience retailers offering prepared foods. Feed costs represent the largest element of production expense and remain volatile. Cage-free production is materially more costly than conventional egg production, and the company notes a limited number of existing cage-free businesses available for acquisition—a constraint as customer demand shifts toward specialty products.

Cal-Maine is executing a multi-pronged expansion strategy. Planned capital expenditure for fiscal 2025 is $53.2 million. The company is adding 1.1 million hens through cage-free layer and pullet house expansion by end of 2025. Post-fiscal year acquisitions include Echo Lake Foods for $258 million and ISE America, which adds 4.7 million laying hen capacity in the Northeast. The company is expanding its MeadowCreek hard-cooked eggs facility and has invested $6.75 million for a 51% stake in Crepini LLC, establishing a venture in egg wraps and protein pancakes.

Greenbrier Companies designs, builds, and leases freight railcars, serving North America as its primary market with secondary operations in Europe, Mexico, and Brazil. The Manufacturing segment designs and constructs freight railcars—including covered hopper cars, gondolas, tank cars, intermodal and automotive cars—in North America and Europe, alongside wheel services, component parts, and maintenance. The Leasing & Fleet Management segment owns and leases a fleet of railcars, primarily sourced from manufacturing, and provides fleet management and regulatory compliance services to railroads and railcar owners. The company positions itself as a leading international supplier with an integrated business model combining manufacturing, leasing, and maintenance that it characterizes as difficult to duplicate. Stated competitive strengths include substantial engineering and technical capabilities, technological leadership in product innovation, and demonstrated ability to capture high market shares across car types.

The company faces material exposure related to the Portland Harbor Superfund Site. In November 2024, the EPA issued a Special Notice Letter to Greenbrier as one of approximately 60 recipients regarding remedial action settlement negotiations; the company responded by the May 30, 2025 deadline and an enforcement moratorium is in effect. The EPA's January 2017 Record of Decision identified a cleanup remedy with an estimated undiscounted cost of $1.7 billion over 13 years of active remediation plus 30 years of monitoring, though responsibility for costs among potentially responsible parties has not yet been determined. Settlement negotiations are expected to continue for up to two years. Additionally, three pending litigation matters relate to the site: Arkema Inc. et al v. A & C Foundry Products, Inc. involves cost allocation among 69 defendants with most signing tolling agreements and being dismissed, with the case stayed through January 14, 2028; the Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation are pursuing a natural resource damages claim without specified amounts; and the company has filed motions to intervene in United States of America et al. v ACF Industries LLC regarding natural resources trustees' claims, with oral argument held September 29, 2025 and a court opinion pending.

Greenbrier faces notable supply and customer concentration risks. Two customers accounted for approximately 26% of consolidated revenue in 2025, with 28% of Manufacturing revenue but only 2% of Leasing & Fleet Management revenue. The top supplier represents 14% of inventory purchases and the top ten suppliers account for 36%. The company sources castings and wheel components through an Amsted-Maxion joint venture in Brazil and operates expanded insourcing capacity in Mexico. Competitive positioning is constrained by the company's position as one of only two largest railcar manufacturers in North America, limiting growth opportunity, and by exposure to government-backed competitors that may sell below cost. A handful of specialty railcar builders compete in niche markets; top-tier manufacturers compete in Europe; and at least twenty institutions provide railcar leasing and services in North America.

Planned capital expenditure totals $320 million. The company is executing restructuring in Europe, including closure of manufacturing facilities in Poland and Turkey completed in Q4 2025 and an announced Romanian closure, alongside a 30% European headcount reduction while maintaining production capacity. A leasing warehouse facility will convert to a term loan in September 2027.

Inspire Medical Systems develops and commercializes the Inspire system, a minimally invasive closed-loop neurostimulation technology for patients with obstructive sleep apnea. The U.S. is the primary market, with secondary presence in Europe, Japan, and Asia Pacific. Inspire positions itself as the first FDA-approved closed-loop neurostimulation therapy for OSA, supported by 385+ peer-reviewed publications, 80% nightly use compliance at five years, and 90% patient satisfaction in registry data. The company claims first-mover advantage with 125,000+ treated patients and a 119-patent intellectual property portfolio. Competition spans multiple therapeutic categories: PAP device manufacturers (ResMed, Philips, Fisher & Paykel), other neurostimulation providers (Nyxoah), surgical alternatives, oral appliances, and emerging pharmaceutical therapies including GLP-1s.

Inspire faces material legal and regulatory headwinds. A Department of Justice Civil Investigative Demand received in January 2025 from the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Minnesota is investigating allegations of false claims and Anti-Kickback Statute violations related to implant procedures, requesting information on marketing, promotion, and reimbursement practices. Separately, six pending litigation matters center on the Inspire V launch: one securities class action (City of Pontiac) was voluntarily dismissed in December 2025, but a second securities class action (Indiana Public Retirement System) remains pending with a motion to transfer to the District of Minnesota; a stockholder derivative lawsuit (Korte v. Herbert) filed January 27, 2026 alleges Section 14(a) and 10(b) violations, breach of fiduciary duty, and unjust enrichment. Additionally, Inspire is engaged in bilateral patent litigation with Nyxoah: Inspire sued in May 2025 alleging the Genio product infringes certain U.S. patents; Nyxoah countersued in September 2025 and again in December 2025 in the Unified Patent Court alleging Inspire IV and V infringe Nyxoah patents. The company took a $4 million impairment charge on a strategic investment and a $2.1 million charge for excess and obsolete Inspire IV inventory in 2025.

The business carries structural vulnerabilities. Certain Inspire system components rely on single-source suppliers, creating supply chain concentration risk that the company identifies as a disadvantage. All manufacturing occurs in the U.S. and most components are U.S.-sourced, limiting geographic diversification. The surgical procedure requirement, while minimally invasive, excludes patients with complete concentric collapse airway anatomy. Reimbursement coverage remains non-uniform across payors. Customer concentration is not acute—no single customer exceeded 10% of 2025 revenue—but international expansion faces longer approval timelines and varied regulatory requirements. Disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting remain effective with no material weaknesses, and the auditor (Ernst & Young) has not changed.

Recent initiatives include the Inspire V launch (FDA approved August 2024, commercial launch May 2025), completion of the PREDICTOR study in early 2024 to eliminate direct endoscopic sleep apnea imaging screening, and the ADHERE patient registry reaching 5,000 patients with follow-up completed in 2025. The company is expanding internationally to South Korea and additional European and Asia Pacific markets. SleepSync platform development continues as a cloud-based patient management system. No specific capex figures or forward revenue guidance were disclosed.

The DOJ separately issued a Request for Additional Information regarding the Getty Images merger on April 2, 2025, and the UK Competition and Markets Authority referred the merger to Phase 2 review in November 2025, creating further uncertainty around transaction closure.

Shutterstock faces a competitive landscape spanning multiple dimensions: established stock content platforms (Getty Images, iStockphoto, AdobeStock, Freepik, 123RF), specialized visual content providers, music publishing entities (Universal Music Publishing Group, Sony/ATV, Warner/Chappell), design and creative workflow tools (Adobe, Canva, Picsart), and generative AI companies (Midjourney, Dall-E, Stable Diffusion, Gemini). The company itself disclosed material disadvantages including low industry barriers to entry, highly competitive and rapidly evolving markets with significant generative AI competition, pricing pressure sensitivity, vulnerability to economic downturns in advertising spend, risk of contributor defection to higher-royalty competitors, dependency on search engine algorithms, and escalating regulatory compliance costs. Customer concentration is diffuse—top 25 customers represent less than 20% of 2025 revenue. Recent acquisitions (Envato, Backgrid in 2024; Giphy in 2023) indicate strategic expansion in content and distribution.

Forward catalysts include the pending Getty Images merger-of-equals transaction, which remains subject to regulatory clearance from the DOJ and UK CMA; expansion of metadata licensing for AI model training; and scaling of Shutterstock Studios custom content and production services. The company uses non-GAAP measures including Adjusted EBITDA, Adjusted net income, and Adjusted free cash flow. No specific capex guidance was provided.

### TMDX [Critical]
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1756262/000119312526067032/tmdx-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: material weakness in internal controls disclosed; 2 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed._
_Chokepoints: 1 cross-corpus connection detected._

TransMedics Group, Inc. develops and operates organ preservation systems and transplant logistics services focused on warm perfusion technology for heart, lung, and liver transplantation. The company's primary business segment comprises its Organ Care System (OCS) platform—which includes OCS Heart, OCS Lung, and OCS Liver devices along with associated consoles and perfusion sets—paired with a National Organ Program that provides organ procurement services and transplant logistics. The United States is the primary market; Europe and Asia-Pacific represent secondary geographies. TransMedics positions itself as the only FDA-approved portable multi-organ warm perfusion platform provider and operates a distinctive integrated model combining owned-and-operated aircraft for organ transportation logistics with clinical expertise in transplant reimbursement and billing. The company claims substantial clinical evidence from large trials and strong relationships with transplant centers and academic medical centers.

TransMedics disclosed a material weakness in internal controls over financial reporting and confirmed that disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) are not effective. Additionally, two pending class action lawsuits allege violations of Sections 10(b) and 20(a) of the Securities Exchange Act. The first lawsuit, Jewik v. TransMedics Group, Inc., filed February 14, 2025, targets purported misstatements and omissions in the 2022 Annual Report, earnings calls, and public statements alleged to have artificially inflated stock price during the period from February 28, 2023 to January 10, 2025. A second suit, Collins v. TransMedics Group, Inc., filed April 2, 2025, asserts similar claims. The cases were consolidated in May 2025, and a consolidated amended complaint was filed on August 8, 2025 seeking unspecified damages; defendants filed a motion to dismiss on October 7, 2025. No financial exposure has been quantified.

The company faces material supply chain dependencies that constrain operational flexibility. Fresenius is the single-source supplier of OCS Solutions for both OCS Lung and OCS Heart platforms. More broadly, components are sourced from third-party suppliers including single-source and sole-source arrangements, creating vulnerability to supply chain disruptions and component price increases. The competitive landscape is fragmented across multiple modalities—including OrganOx Limited, Terumo Corporation, XVIVO Perfusion AB, Paragonix Technologies, and Getinge in cold perfusion and warm perfusion segments, alongside providers of ventricular assist devices, total artificial hearts, normothermic regional perfusion systems, and pharmaceutical therapies. The company acknowledges limited experience operating aircraft and aviation services, dependence on a limited network of organ procurement partners, and the need for continued clinical evidence to drive international reimbursement adoption. Significant upfront costs relative to cold storage preservation and complex manufacturing and sterilization requirements also constrain market penetration.

Forward initiatives include enrollment of 650+ recipients in the ENHANCE Heart trial, launch of the DENOVO Lung trial for superiority claims, and development of a Gen-3 multi-organ platform. TransMedics is constructing R&D and manufacturing facilities in Italy and entered a headquarters lease in Somerville, Massachusetts in January 2026, with base rent commencing in Q1 2028. The company acquired two adjacent parcels of land in Somerville for $15 million each in January 2026 and purchased two parcels in Mirandola, Italy in July 2025 for the planned Italian facility.

### AESI [Critical]
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1984060/000119312526067145/aesi-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: material weakness in internal controls disclosed; 1 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed._

Atlas Energy Solutions Inc. operates two primary business segments serving the oil and gas industry. The Sand and Logistics segment produces and processes proppant—including 100 mesh, 40/70 mesh, 70/140 mesh, and 40/140 mesh sand in dry and damp forms—and operates a logistics platform comprising trucks, trailers, wellsite equipment, and the Dune Express, a 42-mile conveyor system. The Power segment provides distributed power solutions through natural gas-powered reciprocating generators that support production and artificial lift operations. The company is concentrated geographically in the Permian Basin of West Texas and New Mexico, with secondary operations across U.S. resource basins. Atlas positions itself as a low-cost producer with substantial sand reserves (571.3 million tons proven and probable), in-basin production advantages, differentiated logistics capabilities, industry-leading environmental practices, and in-house manufacturing of power equipment.

Atlas disclosed a material weakness in internal controls over financial reporting, though disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting remain effective as of the filing date. The company is defending a derivative and class action complaint filed by Patrick Ayers alleging breach of fiduciary duty related to the Up-C structure corporate reorganization; the matter is currently in discovery with unspecified damages sought. In 2024, a mechanical fire damaged plant assets and equipment at the company's Kermit facility, and a dredge mining asset at the same facility was disposed of after sustaining damage. These operational disruptions occurred against a backdrop of recent acquisition activity: the company acquired Moser Holdings, LLC for $180 million in 2025, BCA HoldCo for $25 million in 2025, and Hi-Crush Holdings, Inc. for $140.1 million in 2024.

The company operates under significant structural constraints. Customer concentration is acute, with the top 10 customers representing 82.4% of revenue, creating substantial revenue risk from customer losses or shifts in spending. Transportation costs exceed 50% of delivered proppant cost, compressing margins in an already highly competitive market with limited geographic spreads. The company relies on a sole key supplier for power generation equipment, introducing supply chain vulnerability. Geographic concentration in the Permian Basin magnifies exposure to regional commodity cycles. The competitive landscape includes established national producers (U.S. Silica Inc., Liberty Energy Inc., Vista Proppants and Logistics, Capital Sand Company), regional competitors (Iron Oak Energy Solutions, Alpine Silica, Badger Mining Corporation), ceramic proppant producers, and alternative power sources ranging from renewable energy to grid providers.

Atlas has reserved 240 megawatts of power generation equipment with late-2026 delivery, acquired PropFlow on-wellsite proppant filtration technology, and is integrating semi-autonomous oilfield logistics capabilities alongside the Moser equipment acquisition. No specific capex guidance was provided.

### AMR [Critical]
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1704715/000170471526000010/amr-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: 1 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed; regulatory action: EPA, EPA and COE._

Alpha Metallurgical Resources, Inc. operates as a single integrated segment focused on mining and selling metallurgical coal to the steel industry, with thermal coal generated as a byproduct. The company extracts coal primarily from mines in Virginia and West Virginia, serving customers across Asia as a primary market and Europe and other Americas regions secondarily. Beyond coal sales, the company generates revenue from equipment sales and rentals, terminal and processing fees, and natural gas sales. The company positions itself on the basis of 294.5 million tons of proven and probable reserves, highly productive cost-competitive mines, a 65% ownership stake in Dominion Terminal Associates export terminal, and a safety incident rate 38% better than the U.S. industry average in 2025. It competes against regional and international coal producers, including Australian and Canadian met coal exporters, as well as against alternative energy sources and steel production methods.

The filing surfaces significant regulatory and litigation exposure. A federal complaint was filed in February 2025 challenging New York's Climate Change Superfund Act as unconstitutional, with the U.S. Department of Justice and EPA filing a similar complaint in May 2025. Additionally, the Mine Safety and Health Administration issued a final rule in April 2024 lowering the permissible exposure limit for respirable crystalline silica to 50 micrograms per cubic meter, with compliance required by April 14, 2025; the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals granted a temporary administrative stay and is considering permanent enforcement suspension. The EPA issued multiple final rules in 2024 and 2025 establishing stringent standards for MATS emissions from coal-fired utilities, greenhouse gas reductions from coal plants, and coal combustion residuals management. The Department of Labor also published a final rule in January 2025 requiring 100% minimum collateral for self-insured black lung obligations. The Corps of Engineers reissued 56 nationwide permits in January 2026 effective through March 15, 2031, governing dredge and fill activities. These regulatory actions collectively address environmental compliance, worker health, financial assurance, and water resource management.

The company faces material operational headwinds reflected in recent facility actions. In November 2025, water inundation at Rolling Thunder mine required recovery and idle costs. The Elk Run mining complex was temporarily idled in November 2024 due to soft met coal pricing, and the Long Branch surface mine was temporarily idled in Q1 2025 for the same reason. Production was reduced at Jerry Fork and Black Eagle mines in 2025 due to weak global steel demand. The filing identifies excess production capacity in the coal industry, currency fluctuations disadvantaging U.S. producers, and declining demand driven by climate change initiatives and shifting power generation away from coal as material competitive disadvantages. Complex and costly mining in Central Appalachia subject to substantial regulatory constraints further constrains operations.

Planned capital expenditure is $158 million (within a range of $148–$168 million). Key forward initiatives include Kingston Wildcat underground mine production commencing in Q1 2026, Dominion Terminal Associates infrastructure upgrades averaging $21 million annually, and anticipated realization of Section 45X metallurgical coal tax credits during 2026–2029. The company provided revenue guidance but did not provide earnings per share guidance.

### ARCB [Critical]
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/894405/000110465926019699/arcb-20251231x10k.htm)_

_Triggers: 1 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed; regulatory action: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)._

ArcBest operates a two-segment transportation and logistics business serving primarily the United States with secondary operations in Canada, Mexico, Puerto Rico, and international markets. The Asset-Based segment, anchored by ABF Freight System, Inc., provides less-than-truckload (LTL) services including standard, time-critical, and guaranteed offerings across North America. The Asset-Light segment, comprising MoLo Solutions, Panther Premium Logistics, and related subsidiaries, delivers logistics services through truckload brokerage, managed transportation, expedite freight, international ocean and air shipping, household goods moving under the U-Pack brand, final mile services, warehousing, and retail logistics. The company positions itself on multimodal flexibility, 40,000+ owned and operated assets, proprietary technology, and end-to-end logistics integration, competing against a broad landscape including FedEx Freight, Knight-Swift, Old Dominion, XPO, J.B. Hunt, and regional carriers across unionized and nonunion segments.

ArcBest disclosed material litigation and regulatory exposure during the period. The company settled lawsuits related to an auto accident involving a MoLo contract carrier and a Fair Labor Standards Act wage classification claim totaling $9.8 million in Q4 2024, with payments made in January 2025. More significantly, ABF Freight entered into a Consent Decree with the Environmental Protection Agency in 2023 to resolve alleged Clean Water Act compliance violations, with no stated monetary amount disclosed. Additionally, the California Air Resources Board issued an enforcement notice related to climate corporate data accountability reporting, with a compliance deadline shifted to August 2026. The company also recorded a $28.7 million impairment in 2024 on an equity investment in Phantom Auto, a remote operation software provider that ceased operations, and a $6.6 million noncash impairment charge to the Panther trade name in 2025, alongside a $5.4 million write-off of obsolete Vaux suite assets.

Customer concentration remains low across all segments: no single customer exceeded 3% of consolidated revenues in the year ended December 31, 2025, with the ten largest customers representing approximately 14% of total revenues. Within Asset-Based, the top ten customers accounted for 17% of segment revenues (4% maximum single customer), and within Asset-Light, 18% (5% maximum single customer). The company explicitly identifies its union carrier cost structure as a structural disadvantage, disclosing higher fringe benefit contributions, wage rates for freight-handling and driving personnel, less stringent labor work rules than nonunion peers, and fixed labor costs that limit staffing flexibility during business cycles. The business is more capital-intensive than certain competitors.

Planned capital expenditure ranges from $150 million to $170 million. Named initiatives include launching the ArcBest View digital platform and ViewPoint visibility tool in the first half of 2026, expanding City Route Optimization technology with city pick-up augmentation phases, conducting service center remodels and facility upgrades, and expanding the Vaux suite with Smart Autonomy and Vision technologies.

### ASTH [Critical]
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1083446/000119312526103128/asth-20251231.htm)_

_Triggers: material weakness in internal controls disclosed; 1 pending litigation matter(s) disclosed._

Astrana Health operates an integrated healthcare delivery and management platform across three interconnected segments. Care Partners builds and manages provider networks through risk-bearing organizations including IPAs and ACOs, managing capitated arrangements across Medicare, Medicaid, Commercial, and Exchange lines. Care Delivery operates over 60 locations encompassing primary care clinics, specialty care, an acute care hospital, urgent care centers, imaging facilities, ambulatory surgery centers, and specialty pharmacy services. Care Enablement provides a proprietary technology platform offering clinical, operational, and financial integration, along with management services including physician recruiting, claims processing, revenue cycle management, and credentialing. The company is primarily based in California with secondary operations in Southern Nevada and multiple other states, positioning itself on integrated clinical, administrative, and technology capabilities at scale, a network of over 20,000 contracted physicians, and population health management expertise.

Astrana disclosed a material weakness in internal controls over financial reporting, indicating deficiencies in the design or operation of controls sufficient to allow misstatement of financial statements. The company's disclosure controls are also not effective. Additionally, a legal matter with a provider associated with CFC HP was recognized as a loss contingency in Q3 2025, with estimated financial exposure of $13 million. These control deficiencies and pending litigation represent substantive risks to financial reporting reliability and potential material liabilities.

The company faces significant structural concentration risk: four payers accounted for 59.8% of total net revenue in the year ended December 31, 2025. Geographic concentration is also notable, with California as the primary market. The company self-discloses exposure to capitation contract losses if expenses exceed revenues and limited control over out-of-network provider behavior in ACO arrangements. It faces physician recruitment and retention pressures in a competitive labor market. Astrana competes against a broad set of regional and national players including Optum, Privia Health, Aledade, Envision Healthcare, and multiple local systems and medical groups. The company carries high indebtedness from Prospect Acquisition financing, completed in July 2025 for $674.9 million, which included acquisition of Foothill Regional Medical Center, an acute care hospital in Tustin, California.

Recent activity includes completion of the Prospect Medical Holdings acquisition in July 2025, a Second Amended Restated Credit Agreement in February 2025, and expansion of partnerships in Southern California and Southern Nevada, including collaboration with Intermountain Health. The company is expanding participation in ACO REACH Model and MSSP programs.

### BANC [Critical]

BANC OF CALIFORNIA operates a regional banking platform centered on California with secondary operations in Colorado and North Carolina. The company spans four segments: Commercial & Community Banking, which conducts in-market relationship lending and deposit gathering across 79 branch locations; Specialty Banking, serving niche verticals including HOA, venture banking, lender finance, SBA lending, mortgage warehouse, media and entertainment, asset-based lending, and equipment finance; Deposit and Transaction Services, offering cash management, treasury management, foreign exchange, and liquidity products; and Payment Solutions, delivering merchant acquiring and card issuing through platforms including BancEdge and SmartStreet. The loan portfolio encompasses commercial real estate, multi-family, residential mortgages, construction, equipment finance, venture capital, warehouse, asset-based, and consumer products. The company positions itself on relationship-based banking with in-depth industry knowledge and flexible structuring, contrasting itself against larger regional and national banks, community banks, venture debt funds, non-bank lenders, fintech firms, and other financial institutions that lack the same regulatory constraints.

BANC OF CALIFORNIA recorded a goodwill impairment charge of $1.376 billion in fiscal 2023 related to the PacWest Bancorp merger integration and balance sheet repositioning. This impairment reflects a significant revaluation of the PacWest acquisition completed in 2023 for $400 million. Simultaneously, the company is executing a strategic loan sale process, transferring $506.7 million to held-for-sale in Q2 2025, following a $1.95 billion Civic loan sale in Q3 2024. The company also faces pending litigation pertaining to fiduciary and other claims connected to the PacWest Merger, though liabilities are believed immaterial based on currently available information.

The company operates with no individual deposit relationship exceeding 10% of total deposits, avoiding material customer concentration risk on the deposit side. However, BANC faces structural disadvantages against larger competitors who hold substantial capital, wider branch networks, lower cost of capital access, and regulatory flexibility. The company's competitive position depends on relationship-based differentiation and niche expertise in specialty verticals, a narrower moat than scale-based competitors possess.

Recent initiatives include a $300 million stock repurchase program covering common and preferred stock and a $500 million FHLB long-term advance at 3.18% to replace higher-cost funding. Ernst & Young LLP serves as auditor, with disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting both effective. The company uses non-GAAP measures including adjusted return on average tangible common equity and adjusted net earnings.

### BFH [Critical]
_[View on SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1101215/000110121526000016/bfh-20251231.htm)_
